summary: Grant County International Airport (MWH) in Moses Lake, Washington, sits on the site of the former Larson Air Force Base, a World War II training field for B-17 and B-24 bomber crews. Its 13,500-foot runway is one of the longest in North America, originally engineered to handle fully loaded heavy bombers and later repurposed for civilian aviation and large aircraft testing, including Boeing 737 programs. Today it serves as a medium-sized hub for general aviation, cargo, and flight testing in the Columbia Basin.
faqs:
Q: Why does Grant County International Airport have such a long runway?
A: The 13,500-foot runway was built during World War II to accommodate heavy bombers like the B-17 and B-24 taking off fully loaded with fuel and ordnance. Today it supports large cargo aircraft, test flights, and serves as an emergency landing site for space shuttle missions historically.

Q: How far is the airport from downtown Moses Lake?
A: The airport is approximately 5 miles (8 km) northwest of downtown Moses Lake, a quick 10-minute drive by car.

Q: Does the airport offer scheduled commercial service?
A: Scheduled commercial passenger service is limited; the airport primarily supports general aviation, corporate flights, cargo operations, and aircraft testing rather than daily commercial routes.

Q: Is rental car service available at the airport?
A: Rental car availability is limited and often requires advance booking; many visitors arrange rentals through providers in Moses Lake town.
transport_tips: Having a personal vehicle is the most practical way to reach the airport, as there is no dedicated public transit link and taxi or rideshare options can be scarce in this rural area. The airport sits off State Route 17, making the drive straightforward from Moses Lake or nearby Ephrata. Allow extra time during winter months, as central Washington can experience freezing fog and icy road conditions.
local_tip: If you're an aviation enthusiast, request to drive down the service road parallel to the main runway for a clear view of its extraordinary length—it's a rare sight in the U.S. and a favorite stop for plane
